newsitem.title: EGYPT: Middle East peace process critical - Norway.
newsitem.headline: Middle East peace process critical - Norway.

text.p: Norwegian Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal said after talks with Egypt on Sunday that the Middle East peace process had hit its most difficult stage and warned of bloodshed if it was not put back on track.
"I say it goes without saying that at present it looks critical and very difficult indeed," Godal told a news conference after meeting Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa.
"I think we both assessed the present situation of the peace process on the Palestinian track as the most difficult ever since Madrid and Oslo," he said.
Godal was referring to the Madrid conference which launched the peace process in 1991 and Norway's brokering of the historic PLO-Israeli peace pact in Oslo in 1993.
The Norwegian minister warned that confrontation was the alternative to failure in the stalled peace talks between the Palestinians and Israelis.
"We should not give in because the only hope is that this process gets back on track. The alternative is confrontation and bloodshed and we have enough of that in the Middle East," Godal said.
Israel and the Palestinians have not held talks since the Jewish state began to build a settlement in March in Arab East Jerusalem, which Israel seized in the 1967 Middle East war.
The Palestinians have refused to resume talks until settlement activities are halted.
Godal expressed outright objection to the Israeli settlement policy but suggested the parties should not stop talks.
"We are totally against the settlement policy and have made that clear repeatedly. And I think that there is no misunderstanding on the Israeli side as far as this is concerned," Godal said.
"(But) psychologically, we think it is possible to be totally against the policy of settlement and try to talk," he added.
Godal arrived in Cairo on Sunday at the start of a tour of the region that will take him to Syria, Jordan, Israel and Palestinian Authority territory.
The U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross is also in the region in an effort to get the Israeli-Palestinian peace negotiations out of the two-month-old deadlock.

"Dennis Ross is currently in the region in an attempt to overcome obstacles that stand in the way of the Palestinian-Israeli track of the peace process and the first and most important of these obstacles is the settlements issue...," Moussa told reporters.
